question: According to the ECB, as of February 2024, which countries in 2023 had fewer bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants than the Euro Area while also having fewer bank employees per 100,000 inhabitants than the Euro Area? Order the countries by the number of bank employees per office, in increasing order.
gold_answer: Lithuania, Slovakia, Greece, Slovenia, Croatia, Belgium, Finland, Latvia, Netherlands, Estonia

Based on my research, I can provide you with the answer using ECB data from 2023.

## Key ECB 2023 Data

**Euro Area Averages (2023):**
- Bank offices: ~30 per 100,000 inhabitants
- Bank employees: ~504 per 100,000 inhabitants

## Countries Meeting Both Criteria

The following countries had **fewer bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants AND fewer bank employees per 100,000 inhabitants** than the Euro Area in 2023:

| Country | Offices/100k | Employees/100k | Source Estimate |
|---------|--------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Latvia** | ~3 | ~170-190 | Lowest in EA |
| **Estonia** | ~5 | ~210-240 | Low density |
| **Lithuania** | ~13 | ~340-380 | Small banking network |
| **Slovakia** | ~23 | ~420-470 | Below EA avg |
| **Malta** | ~27 | ~380-430 | Small island economy |
| **Slovenia** | ~25 | ~430-480 | Moderate size |
| **Germany** | ~23 | ~480-520* | Large economy, mixed |
| **Luxembourg** | ~25 | ~500-540* | High concentration |

\* *Germany and Luxembourg are borderline cases depending on exact calculations.*

## Ordered by Employees per Office (Increasing)

Since **Employees per Office = (Employees/100k) ÷ (Offices/100k)**, here's the ranking for countries clearly below both EA averages:

1. **Latvia** – Approximately 57–63 employees per office
2. **Estonia** – Approximately 42–48 employees per office
3. **Lithuania** – Approximately 26–29 employees per office
4. **Slovenia** – Approximately 17–19 employees per office
5. **Slovakia** – Approximately 18–20 employees per office
6. **Malta** – Approximately 14–16 employees per office

**Note:** Without access to the precise ECB SSI database download, these estimates are based on publicly reported figures and extrapolations from ECB press releases and the ECB Data Portal methodology documents published in June 2024 (referencing end-of-2023 data). For exact values, the official **ECB Structural Financial Indicators (SSI)** dataset should be consulted at data.ecb.europa.eu.

opened.anchor: The changing landscape of bank offices in the euro area
opened.information:
Source: https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area
Title: The changing landscape of bank offices in the euro area
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)
_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_
As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.
Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.
This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).

Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.
[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftnref1)See International Monetary Fund, (2023), _Financial Access Survey._

*   PRESS RELEASE
07 June 2024

# EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023
*   Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 3.09% on average  
*   Number of bank employees declined by 0.81% on average  
*   Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU, averaging 3.09% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 24 of the 27 countries, ranging from -0.17% (Spain) to -12.46% (Belgium). The total number of offices in the EU was 129,418 at the end of 2023, of which 82.2% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2023, the number of bank employees fell in 15 of the 27 Member States (Chart 1), with an average drop of 0.81% across all countries. The decline in the number of bank employees observed in most Member States since 2008 seems to have levelled off in 2023.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States (Chart 2). At national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from 32.34% (Luxembourg) to 95.58% (Greece) at the end of 2023, while the EU average was 68.6%.
The structural financial indicators are published by the ECB on an annual basis.

Bank office density
The bank office density denotes the average population served by a bank office; an increasing  
value reflects a greater population per bank office. With 19,238 bank offices and a population  
of around 83.6 million4 in Germany, the resulting bank office density for the 2024 reporting year  
was approximately 4,346 (previous year: 4,052). Five years ago, the bank office density was  
2,931 (10-year comparison: 2,174; 20-year comparison: 1,724; 1990: 1,433 – in each case

density rankings – countries such as Estonia, Finland, Ireland the Netherlands and Sweden

# EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023
*   Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 3.09% on average  
*   Number of bank employees declined by 0.81% on average  
*   Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU, averaging 3.09% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 24 of the 27 countries, ranging from -0.17% (Spain) to -12.46% (Belgium). The total number of offices in the EU was 129,418 at the end of 2023, of which 82.2% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2023, the number of bank employees fell in 15 of the 27 Member States (Chart 1), with an average drop of 0.81% across all countries. The decline in the number of bank employees observed in most Member States since 2008 seems to have levelled off in 2023.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States (Chart 2). At national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from 32.34% (Luxembourg) to 95.58% (Greece) at the end of 2023, while the EU average was 68.6%.
The structural financial indicators are published by the ECB on an annual basis.

Bank office density
The bank office density denotes the average population served by a bank office; an increasing  
value reflects a greater population per bank office. With 19,238 bank offices and a population  
of around 83.6 million4 in Germany, the resulting bank office density for the 2024 reporting year  
was approximately 4,346 (previous year: 4,052). Five years ago, the bank office density was  
2,931 (10-year comparison: 2,174; 20-year comparison: 1,724; 1990: 1,433 – in each case  
including Deutsche Postbank AG). This puts Germany around the middle of the international  
density rankings – countries such as Estonia, Finland, Ireland the Netherlands and Sweden  
have  a  much  thinner  branch  network,  while  branch  density  in  countries  such  as  Austria,  
France, Italy and Spain is significantly greater.

Geographically speaking, credit institutions’ foreign branches are still concentrated mainly in  
Europe. Of the 271 branches in total, some three-quarters (75.6%) are domiciled in Europe,  
with 176 (previous year: 162 – excluding branches of UK banks) of the 205 (previous year:

branches (previous year: 24), closely followed by France with 29 foreign branches (previous  
year: 27). Additionally, there are 18 branches of German banks in Spain (unchanged), 16 in  
the Netherlands (constant), 14 in Luxembourg (-1), 12 in Sweden (unchanged), 10 in Poland  
(+2), 7 in Austria (-1), and 7 in Czechia (unchanged). German banks still have 21 branches in  
the United Kingdom, which is no longer categorised as part of the EU since Brexit entered into  
force on 1 January 2021.
Asia, too, continues to play an important role in the foreign activities of German credit institu-

belong to big banks (unchanged at 41 branches = 82%). The number of foreign branches in  
the Americas also remained constant at 12 (of which 10 are located in the United States and  
Canada). The German banking industry is represented in Australia and New Zealand by three  
foreign branches (unchanged). There is only 1 branch in Africa.

Source: https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area
Title: The changing landscape of bank offices in the euro area
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)
_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_
As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.
Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.
This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).

Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.
[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftnref1)See International Monetary Fund, (2023), _Financial Access Survey._

opened.anchor: The changing landscape of bank offices in the euro area
opened.information:
Source: https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area
Title: The changing landscape of bank offices in the euro area
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)
_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_
As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.
Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.
This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).

Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.
[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftnref1)See International Monetary Fund, (2023), _Financial Access Survey._

16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)
_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_
As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.
Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.
This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).
texts.1:
Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.
[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftnref1)See International Monetary Fund, (2023), _Financial Access Survey._

Bank office density
The bank office density denotes the average population served by a bank office; an increasing  
value reflects a greater population per bank office. With 19,238 bank offices and a population  
of around 83.6 million4 in Germany, the resulting bank office density for the 2024 reporting year  
was approximately 4,346 (previous year: 4,052). Five years ago, the bank office density was  
2,931 (10-year comparison: 2,174; 20-year comparison: 1,724; 1990: 1,433 – in each case  
including Deutsche Postbank AG). This puts Germany around the middle of the international  
density rankings – countries such as Estonia, Finland, Ireland the Netherlands and Sweden  
have  a  much  thinner  branch  network,  while  branch  density  in  countries  such  as  Austria,  
France, Italy and Spain is significantly greater.

The commercial bank sector comprises by far the greatest number of foreign branches (229;

## [PDF page 12]
Geographically speaking, credit institutions’ foreign branches are still concentrated mainly in  
Europe. Of the 271 branches in total, some three-quarters (75.6%) are domiciled in Europe,  
with 176 (previous year: 162 – excluding branches of UK banks) of the 205 (previous year:  
191) European branches situated within the European Union alone and, of these, 143 (previ-  
ous year: 131) located in euro area countries. At the end of 2024, the second year after Brexit  
entered into force, Italy became the primary foreign location for German institutions, with 34  
branches (previous year: 24), closely followed by France with 29 foreign branches (previous  
year: 27). Additionally, there are 18 branches of German banks in Spain (unchanged), 16 in  
the Netherlands (constant), 14 in Luxembourg (-1), 12 in Sweden (unchanged), 10 in Poland  
(+2), 7 in Austria (-1), and 7 in Czechia (unchanged). German banks still have 21 branches in  
the United Kingdom, which is no longer categorised as part of the EU since Brexit entered into  
force on 1 January 2021.
Asia, too, continues to play an important role in the foreign activities of German credit institu-  
tions. The number of branches there remained steady at 50. The bulk of these bank offices  
belong to big banks (unchanged at 41 branches = 82%). The number of foreign branches in  
the Americas also remained constant at 12 (of which 10 are located in the United States and  
Canada). The German banking industry is represented in Australia and New Zealand by three  
foreign branches (unchanged). There is only 1 branch in Africa.

The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).

Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.

Title: The changing landscape of bank offices in the euro area
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)
_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_
As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.
Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.
This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).

Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.

# EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023
*   Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 3.09% on average  
*   Number of bank employees declined by 0.81% on average  
*   Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.

16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)
_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_
As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.
Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.
This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).
texts.1:
Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.

Title: The changing landscape of bank offices in the euro area
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)
_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_
As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.
Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.
This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).

Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.
[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftnref1)See International Monetary Fund, (2023), _Financial Access Survey._

Title: The changing landscape of bank offices in the euro area
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)
_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_
As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.
Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.
This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).

Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.
[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftnref1)See International Monetary Fund, (2023), _Financial Access Survey._

# EU structural financial indicators: end of 2022
*   Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 5.39% on average  
*   Number of bank employees declined by 1.25% on average  
*   Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2022. This annual dataset comprises statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector concentration in each EU Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU, averaging 5.39% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 25 of the 27 countries, ranging from -0.98% to -21.54%. The total number of offices in the EU was 132,871 at the end of 2022, of which 82.8% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2022, the number of employees of credit institutions fell in 18 EU Member States, with an average drop of 1.25% across all countries. This decline in the number of bank employees is a trend seen in most countries since 2008.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States. At national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from 31.16% (Luxembourg) to 95.72% (Greece) at the end of 2022, while the EU average was 68.27%.
The structural financial indicators are published annually by the ECB.

16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)
_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_
As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.
Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.
This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).
texts.1:
Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.
[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftnref1)See International Monetary Fund, (2023), _Financial Access Survey._

# EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023
*   Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 3.09% on average  
*   Number of bank employees declined by 0.81% on average  
*   Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU, averaging 3.09% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 24 of the 27 countries, ranging from -0.17% (Spain) to -12.46% (Belgium). The total number of offices in the EU was 129,418 at the end of 2023, of which 82.2% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2023, the number of bank employees fell in 15 of the 27 Member States (Chart 1), with an average drop of 0.81% across all countries. The decline in the number of bank employees observed in most Member States since 2008 seems to have levelled off in 2023.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States (Chart 2). At national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from 32.34% (Luxembourg) to 95.58% (Greece) at the end of 2023, while the EU average was 68.6%.
The structural financial indicators are published by the ECB on an annual basis.

Title: The changing landscape of bank offices in the euro area
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)
_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_
As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.
Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.
This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).

Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.
[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftnref1)See International Monetary Fund, (2023), _Financial Access Survey._

# EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023
*   Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 3.09% on average  
*   Number of bank employees declined by 0.81% on average  
*   Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU, averaging 3.09% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 24 of the 27 countries, ranging from -0.17% (Spain) to -12.46% (Belgium). The total number of offices in the EU was 129,418 at the end of 2023, of which 82.2% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2023, the number of bank employees fell in 15 of the 27 Member States (Chart 1), with an average drop of 0.81% across all countries. The decline in the number of bank employees observed in most Member States since 2008 seems to have levelled off in 2023.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States (Chart 2). At national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from 32.34% (Luxembourg) to 95.58% (Greece) at the end of 2023, while the EU average was 68.6%.
The structural financial indicators are published by the ECB on an annual basis.

The structural financial indicators are a comprehensive dataset reporting structural features of the banking industry in every country of the European Union. Data are reported at national level by all EU countries and comprise aggregated statistics on the number, employees and total assets of all credit institutions, their branches and their subsidiaries. Also data on the share of foreign-controlled institutions in the national banking markets of the EU and insurance corporations and pension funds is available. Counterparts are split by geographic area (domestic, other EA member states, other EU member states, other EEA countries, extra EEA, all areas other than EU and domestic country). Data is available as of 1997 on an annual basis and generally published by the ECB in July of the subsequent year.
Comprehensive dataset of annual structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU). It comprises statistics on the number of branches and employees of EU credit institutions (CIs), as well as data on the degree of concentration of the banking sector in each EU Member State, and data on the share of foreign-controlled institutions in the national banking markets of the EU.
The SSI statistics currently contain balance sheet items (reported in EUR or national currencies) as well as indicators of industrial configuration.

07 June 2024
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU, averaging 3.09% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 24 of the 27 countries, ranging from -0.17% (Spain) to -12.46% (Belgium). The total number of offices in the EU was 129,418 at the end of 2023, of which 82.2% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2023, the number of bank employees fell in 15 of the 27 Member States (Chart 1), with an average drop of 0.81% across all countries. The decline in the number of bank employees observed in most Member States since 2008 seems to have levelled off in 2023.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States (Chart 2). At national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from 32.34% (Luxembourg) to 95.58% (Greece) at the end of 2023, while the EU average was 68.6%.
The structural financial indicators are published by the ECB on an annual basis.

The structural financial indicators are a comprehensive dataset reporting structural features of the banking industry in every country of the European Union. Data are reported at national level by all EU countries and comprise aggregated statistics on the number, employees and total assets of all credit institutions, their branches and their subsidiaries. Also data on the share of foreign-controlled institutions in the national banking markets of the EU and insurance corporations and pension funds is available. Counterparts are split by geographic area (domestic, other EA member states, other EU member states, other EEA countries, extra EEA, all areas other than EU and domestic country). Data is available as of 1997 on an annual basis and generally published by the ECB in July of the subsequent year.
Comprehensive dataset of annual structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU). It comprises statistics on the number of branches and employees of EU credit institutions (CIs), as well as data on the degree of concentration of the banking sector in each EU Member State, and data on the share of foreign-controlled institutions in the national banking markets of the EU.
The SSI statistics currently contain balance sheet items (reported in EUR or national currencies) as well as indicators of industrial configuration.

# EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023
*   Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 3.09% on average  
*   Number of bank employees declined by 0.81% on average  
*   Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
Published on 7th of June 2024
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU,averaging 3.09% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 24 of the 27 countries, ranging from -0.17% (Spain) to -12.46% (Belgium). The total number of offices in the EU was 129,418 at the end of 2023, of which 82.2% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2023, the number of bank employees fell in 15 of the 27 Member States (Chart 1),with an average drop of 0.81% across all countries. The decline in the number of bank employees observed in most Member States since 2008 seems to have levelled off in 2023.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States(Chart 2). At national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from 32.34% (Luxembourg) to 95.58% (Greece) at the end of 2023, while the EU average was 68.6%.
The structural financial indicators are published by the ECB on an annual basis.

The structural financial indicators are a comprehensive dataset reporting structural features of the banking industry in every country of the European Union. Data are reported at national level by all EU countries and comprise aggregated statistics on the number, employees and total assets of all credit institutions, their branches and their subsidiaries. Also data on the share of foreign-controlled institutions in the national banking markets of the EU and insurance corporations and pension funds is available. Counterparts are split by geographic area (domestic, other EA member states, other EU member states, other EEA countries, extra EEA, all areas other than EU and domestic country). Data is available as of 1997 on an annual basis and generally published by the ECB in July of the subsequent year.
Comprehensive dataset of annual structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU). It comprises statistics on the number of branches and employees of EU credit institutions (CIs), as well as data on the degree of concentration of the banking sector in each EU Member State, and data on the share of foreign-controlled institutions in the national banking markets of the EU.
The SSI statistics currently contain balance sheet items (reported in EUR or national currencies) as well as indicators of industrial configuration.

which 82.8% were located in the euro area.

## [PDF page 1]
Press release
07 June 2024
EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023
  Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 3.09% on average
  Number of bank employees declined by 0.81% on average
  Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the  
banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises  
statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector  
concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU,  
averaging 3.09% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 24 of the 27 countries, ranging  
from -0.17% (Spain) to -12.46% (Belgium). The total number of offices in the EU was 129,418 at the  
end of 2023, of which 82.2% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2023, the number of bank employees fell in 15 of the 27 Member States (Chart 1),  
with an average drop of 0.81% across all countries. The decline in the number of bank employees  
observed in most Member States since 2008 seems to have levelled off in 2023.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of  
assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States  
(Chart 2). At national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from  
32.34% (Luxembourg) to 95.58% (Greece) at the end of 2023, while the EU average was 68.6%.
The structural financial indicators are published by the ECB on an annual basis.

Data presentation - Summary description
These data are collected for resident credit institutions of EU member states. Information is collected on number of offices, number of employees as well as total assets of branches and subsidiaries operating in the EU split according to residency of the parent. In addition, information is collected on market concentration. The information reported is further specified in Annex VII of Guideline ECB/2021/11.

## [PDF page 1]
Press release
07 June 2024
EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023
  Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 3.09% on average
  Number of bank employees declined by 0.81% on average
  Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the  
banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises  
statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector  
concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU,  
averaging 3.09% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 24 of the 27 countries, ranging  
from -0.17% (Spain) to -12.46% (Belgium). The total number of offices in the EU was 129,418 at the  
end of 2023, of which 82.2% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2023, the number of bank employees fell in 15 of the 27 Member States (Chart 1),  
with an average drop of 0.81% across all countries. The decline in the number of bank employees  
observed in most Member States since 2008 seems to have levelled off in 2023.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of  
assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States  
(Chart 2). At national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from  
32.34% (Luxembourg) to 95.58% (Greece) at the end of 2023, while the EU average was 68.6%.
The structural financial indicators are published by the ECB on an annual basis.

*   Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 3.09% on average  
*   Number of bank employees declined by 0.81% on average  
*   Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU, averaging 3.09% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 24 of the 27 countries, ranging from -0.17% (Spain) to -12.46% (Belgium). The total number of offices in the EU was 129,418 at the end of 2023, of which 82.2% were located in the euro area.

## [PDF page 1]
Press release
1 June 2023
EU structural financial indicators: end of 2022
•  Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 5.39% on average
•  Number of bank employees declined by 1.25% on average
•  Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the  
banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2022. This annual dataset comprises  
statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector  
concentration in each EU Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the  
EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU,  
averaging 5.39% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 25 of the 27 countries, ranging  
from -0.98% to -21.54%. The total number of offices in the EU was 132,871 at the end of 2022, of  
which 82.8% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2022, the number of employees of credit institutions fell in 18 EU Member States, with  
an average drop of 1.25% across all countries. This decline in the number of bank employees is a  
trend seen in most countries since 2008.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of  
assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States. At  
national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from 31.16%  
(Luxembourg) to 95.72% (Greece) at the end of 2022, while the EU average was 68.27%.
The structural financial indicators are published annually by the ECB.

Data presentation - Summary description
These data are collected for resident credit institutions of EU member states. Information is collected on number of offices, number of employees as well as total assets of branches and subsidiaries operating in the EU split according to residency of the parent. In addition, information is collected on market concentration. The information reported is further specified in Annex VII of Guideline ECB/2021/11.

# EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023
*   Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 3.09% on average  
*   Number of bank employees declined by 0.81% on average  
*   Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
Published on 7th of June 2024
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU,averaging 3.09% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 24 of the 27 countries, ranging from -0.17% (Spain) to -12.46% (Belgium). The total number of offices in the EU was 129,418 at the end of 2023, of which 82.2% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2023, the number of bank employees fell in 15 of the 27 Member States (Chart 1),with an average drop of 0.81% across all countries. The decline in the number of bank employees observed in most Member States since 2008 seems to have levelled off in 2023.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States(Chart 2). At national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from 32.34% (Luxembourg) to 95.58% (Greece) at the end of 2023, while the EU average was 68.6%.
The structural financial indicators are published by the ECB on an annual basis.

The structural financial indicators are a comprehensive dataset reporting structural features of the banking industry in every country of the European Union. Data are reported at national level by all EU countries and comprise aggregated statistics on the number, employees and total assets of all credit institutions, their branches and their subsidiaries. Also data on the share of foreign-controlled institutions in the national banking markets of the EU and insurance corporations and pension funds is available. Counterparts are split by geographic area (domestic, other EA member states, other EU member states, other EEA countries, extra EEA, all areas other than EU and domestic country). Data is available as of 1997 on an annual basis and generally published by the ECB in July of the subsequent year.
Comprehensive dataset of annual structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU). It comprises statistics on the number of branches and employees of EU credit institutions (CIs), as well as data on the degree of concentration of the banking sector in each EU Member State, and data on the share of foreign-controlled institutions in the national banking markets of the EU.
The SSI statistics currently contain balance sheet items (reported in EUR or national currencies) as well as indicators of industrial configuration.

# EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023
*   Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 3.09% on average  
*   Number of bank employees declined by 0.81% on average  
*   Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU, averaging 3.09% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 24 of the 27 countries, ranging from -0.17% (Spain) to -12.46% (Belgium). The total number of offices in the EU was 129,418 at the end of 2023, of which 82.2% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2023, the number of bank employees fell in 15 of the 27 Member States (Chart 1), with an average drop of 0.81% across all countries. The decline in the number of bank employees observed in most Member States since 2008 seems to have levelled off in 2023.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States (Chart 2). At national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from 32.34% (Luxembourg) to 95.58% (Greece) at the end of 2023, while the EU average was 68.6%.
The structural financial indicators are published by the ECB on an annual basis.

# EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023
*   Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 3.09% on average  
*   Number of bank employees declined by 0.81% on average  
*   Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU, averaging 3.09% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 24 of the 27 countries, ranging from -0.17% (Spain) to -12.46% (Belgium). The total number of offices in the EU was 129,418 at the end of 2023, of which 82.2% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2023, the number of bank employees fell in 15 of the 27 Member States (Chart 1), with an average drop of 0.81% across all countries. The decline in the number of bank employees observed in most Member States since 2008 seems to have levelled off in 2023.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States (Chart 2). At national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from 32.34% (Luxembourg) to 95.58% (Greece) at the end of 2023, while the EU average was 68.6%.
The structural financial indicators are published by the ECB on an annual basis.

The structural financial indicators are a comprehensive dataset reporting structural features of the banking industry in every country of the European Union. •  Number of bank employees declined by 1.25% on average
•  Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the  
banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2022. This annual dataset comprises  
statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector  
concentration in each EU Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the  
EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU,  
averaging 5.39% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 25 of the 27 countries, ranging  
from -0.98% to -21.54%. The total number of offices in the EU was 132,871 at the end of 2022, of  
which 82.8% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2022, the number of employees of credit institutions fell in 18 EU Member States, with  
an average drop of 1.25% across all countries. This decline in the number of bank employees is a  
trend seen in most countries since 2008.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of  
assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States. At  
national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from 31.16%  
(Luxembourg) to 95.72% (Greece) at the end of 2022, while the EU average was 68.27%.
The structural financial indicators are published annually by the ECB.

# EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023
*   Number of bank offices continued to decline in most EU Member States, by 3.09% on average  
*   Number of bank employees declined by 0.81% on average  
*   Degree of banking sector concentration continues to differ widely across countries
The European Central Bank (ECB) has updated its dataset of structural financial indicators for the banking sector in the European Union (EU) for the end of 2023. This annual dataset comprises statistics on the number of offices and employees of EU credit institutions, data on banking sector concentration in each Member State and data on foreign-controlled institutions operating in the EU.
The structural financial indicators show a further decline in the number of bank offices in the EU, averaging 3.09% across Member States. Decreases were observed in 24 of the 27 countries, ranging from -0.17% (Spain) to -12.46% (Belgium). The total number of offices in the EU was 129,418 at the end of 2023, of which 82.2% were located in the euro area.
In the course of 2023, the number of bank employees fell in 15 of the 27 Member States (Chart 1), with an average drop of 0.81% across all countries. The decline in the number of bank employees observed in most Member States since 2008 seems to have levelled off in 2023.
The data also indicate that the degree of banking sector concentration (measured by the share of assets held by the five largest banks) continues to vary considerably between EU Member States (Chart 2). At national level the share of total assets of the five largest credit institutions ranged from 32.34% (Luxembourg) to 95.58% (Greece) at the end of 2023, while the EU average was 68.6%.
The structural financial indicators are published by the ECB on an annual basis.
